public_rationale: The adoption claim has evidence on both sides. Census data from 2024 support him: only about 5% of US firms, and under 8% of the largest firms, reported using AI to produce goods or services. Other 2024 evidence contradicts 'little to suggest' widespread adoption. Microsoft said in October 2024 that nearly 70% of the Fortune 500 used Microsoft 365 Copilot, and McKinsey's 2024 survey found 65% of respondents' organizations regularly used generative AI. So the claim holds for firms across the whole economy but not for large enterprises. On money, reported 2024 estimates put OpenAI's inference spending around $4B against $3.5B to $4.5B of revenue. That fits his loss framing, but no source measures a loss on each prompt, so that part stays unconfirmed.
limitations: Census BTOS counts any AI use, not only generative AI software.
Microsoft's 70% figure counts firms with any Copilot use, not broad deployment, and is a vendor claim.
The McKinsey figure comes from a news report because McKinsey's pages would not load.
The OpenAI cost figures are press estimates.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: ChatGPT loses OpenAI money on every prompt, and there is little evidence of widespread adoption of generative AI software.

statement.excerpt: Yes, there are people that use ChatGPT — 200 million of them a week, allegedly, losing the company money with every prompt — but there is little to suggest that there's widespread adoption of actual generative AI software.

from_speaker: people that use ChatGPT, 200 million of them a week, allegedly
losing the company money with every prompt
little to suggest that there's widespread adoption
our_interpretation: He describes an ongoing state as of the post (December 2024) and names no period. I use calendar 2024 up to the post date, the most recent period public evidence could cover before he wrote.
I read 'losing the company money with every prompt' in its plain sense: serving ChatGPT cost OpenAI more than it brought in. I do not read it as a measured per-prompt figure.

I read 'actual generative AI software' as he sets it up: generative AI products that businesses adopt and pay for (his example is Microsoft Copilot), as distinct from consumer ChatGPT use, which he concedes.
I read 'widespread' as broad uptake across businesses, shown by surveys or vendor disclosures from 2024.
criteria.support_condition: Evidence from 2024 shows that ChatGPT's serving costs exceeded its revenue, and that business adoption of generative AI software was low, for example a single-digit share of firms.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Evidence from 2024 shows that ChatGPT served users profitably, or that business adoption of generative AI software was broad, for example most large firms deploying it.

evidence.excerpt: bi-weekly estimates of AI use rate rose from 3.7% to 5.4%, with an expected rate of about 6.6% by early Fall 2024.
evidence.explanation: In 2024, only about 5% of US firms reported using any AI to produce goods or services. This supports the claim that adoption was not widespread.

evidence.excerpt: The largest size class (250+ employees) exhibits the highest use rate, rising from 5.2% to 7.8% over time
evidence.explanation: Even among the largest firms, the Census AI use rate stayed under 8% through August 2024. This supports the claim of limited adoption.

evidence.excerpt: All-up, nearly 70% of the Fortune 500 now use Microsoft 365 Copilot
evidence.locator: Satya Nadella prepared remarks, Microsoft 365 Copilot section
evidence.explanation: Microsoft said that most of the largest US companies used its paid generative AI product, the very product he names. This cuts against 'little to suggest' widespread adoption among big businesses, though seat counts are not given.

evidence.excerpt: 65 percent of organisations regularly use Gen AI for at least one business function, up from one-third last year.
evidence.explanation: A large 2024 industry survey reported regular generative AI use at most respondents' organizations. That is evidence pointing toward widespread adoption.

evidence.excerpt: This year, OpenAI is likely to spend around $4 billion on processing power supplied by Microsoft
evidence.explanation: Estimated 2024 inference spending (about $4B) was close to or above OpenAI's estimated revenue of $3.5B to $4.5B, with ChatGPT at about $2B of that. This fits his loss framing but does not measure a loss on each prompt.

public_payload.what_would_resolve: Audited or disclosed 2024 figures splitting ChatGPT's serving cost from its revenue, plus one agreed measure of business adoption of generative AI software.
